The Mosquito Net: A Story of Poverty, Helplessness, and the Will to Survive

Mostafa Auvi (মোস্তফা অভি) · 2026-10-31

The Mosquito Net

Finish Prashanta Mridha's "Moshari" and you feel the story has been about a mosquito net and a mosquito all along, and yet about far more than either. Mridha tells of a life that is itself a torn mosquito net: pain slipping in through every gap, bite marks across the whole body, and from the outside, the look of a place where nothing is happening. Saiful's life is like lying curled on a narrow bed with no room to turn. He must go on living regardless, put up with the bites, get up at dawn, wash, and hurry to the hotel for twenty-five taka a day.

The story opens on a small daily torment. It is the same as every night, and tonight again no position feels right. Mridha draws the scene without ornament. The bed is a single cot with planks joined on to make a "semi-double", and it is more than furniture. It is a shape of Saiful's life: two separate things bolted together, unsteady, and still the place where two people spend their nights. There is no room to shift left or right, so Saiful lies on his side with his wife's neck cradled in his left arm. Just then a mosquito drives its spear into the nape of his neck. Perhaps he was about to say something tender to her, but the sting wipes the words out. Poverty works here like an invisible censor. It takes away even a husband and wife's right to whisper to each other. An "ouch" escapes through his cracked lips, he swings his right hand round and slaps, and all that comes of it is a sharp clap. The mosquito goes humming past his ear, as it always does. That "as it always does" carries weight. A man pours his anger, helplessness and shame into one swing, and the mosquito is untouched. It could stand for Saiful's whole life: however hard he tries, his problems stay calm and immovable.

In the middle of this misery, a riddle from primary school comes back to him: "A room inside a room, and inside it you lie down and die." A classmate had told it to him, and he could not answer then. Mridha brings the riddle in without any show of cleverness, as something intimate and homely. Saiful knows the answer now because his life is the answer. A room like a chicken coop beside an open drain, inside it a leaky two-pitched roof of wood, bamboo, matting and palm leaf, and in that room he lies, dying slowly. Then comes his thought: "Even dying is no comfort, so where would I go?" He thinks of death neither as a philosopher nor as a romantic, but in a flat, practical voice. With a net hanging over him that has a dozen or more holes, where is peace supposed to come from, even in death? It might have been funny, but no laughter comes. Inside it you can hear a tired, resentful, ashamed man asking himself: if even death is like this, where is the pleasure in living?

Saiful does not treat his situation as a grand tragedy. If anything, he jokes about it: "Did I ever think I'd end up sleeping on a bed made 'double' out of cheap sawmill planks!" The line holds sharp wit and deep hurt together. He never states his pain outright. He talks about the bed. He does not wail, he mocks, he laughs, he sidesteps. And it is in that sidestepping that the real pain shows through more clearly.

Saiful's past arrives in fragments, but the fragments add up to a steady descent. Eight or ten years ago he was reading English honours at Brajalal College, and his friends called him Saif. Are that Saif and today's Saiful the same man? Mridha is not after nostalgia. He wants to show how a person comes down, step by step. While still a student, Saiful fell in love with Runu and left home. His father disowned him: "The feud of our clan, and it falls on the children!" That single sentence holds a whole social reality. The break between father and son came not only from love but from the politics of the clan, and Saiful became its casualty and began to slide. He found a job at the Shipping Corporation, but within six months the office moved to Chattogram and he was out of work again. Then came waiter's work at an "international standard" hotel in Khulna, where, worn down by the manager's abuse, he grabbed the man by the collar one day, and when an accusation of skimming money was thrown at him, he lashed out at the man and lost the job. With no work anywhere, he left Khulna for Bagerhat and ended up in this hotel, doing everything, manager, waiter and errand boy, at twenty-five taka a day.

Mridha tells this fall at a strangely detached pace. There is no lingering and no surplus emotion. Saiful himself seems no longer to dwell on it, and recites these events like someone reading an old scrap of paper. Yet the pain lands harder because of that flatness. When a man feels nothing more about his own decline, it means the decline has set so deep in him that he can no longer even recognise the pain as pain. It is a kind of exhaustion, and probably the most frightening thing about Saiful.

The account of his daily life is strikingly real. In the morning, four rotis dunked in the gravy of lotpoti or of gizzard and liver. At noon, rice, and a piece of fish if he is lucky, otherwise a few broken scraps, with thick red gravy. At half past eleven at night he comes home, having eaten the noon fare again for supper, with twenty-five taka in his hand. None of this is only about food. It is about dignity. A man who once read English honours now ends his night on leftovers from midday. Mridha offers no commentary. He writes only: "The thick red gravy, at least, you can have as much of as you like." There is bitter irony in "as much as you like," or perhaps not irony at all, just a quiet truth. A man unused to abundance takes whatever he gets as enough, and inside that "enough" lies a kind of surrender.

Four or five Fridays a month the hotel is shut, so the daily wage comes to about six hundred by month's end. Out of it, a hundred and twenty-five taka goes to the landlord for the room beside the open drain and for a sixty-watt bulb allowed until ten at night. What is left must carry husband and wife through the month, and their tongues almost hang out by the end. Mridha does not belabour the sums, and what he does give is enough for the whole picture. A tongue hanging out belongs to hunger, not just to suffering, and the hunger is not only of the stomach. It is hunger for respect, for love, for a life worth living. All of it seems to push out together as one tongue, and Saiful keeps it pressed down inside him and gets on with his day.

Another scene: a mosquito skips the bone below his knee and plants its spear in the soft flesh. He shakes his leg, and when the mosquito will not budge he swings his hand down hard. A mosquito swollen with blood leaves something thick and sticky on his palm. Then he wonders whether it bit through the trouser cloth or whether the trousers have a hole, and he sweeps his hand over the fabric as if searching for mustard seeds. If a mosquito can drink through his trousers, his manhood has been shattered by a mosquito. What he feels here is less pain than shame, shame before a mosquito, and it shows how far his self-respect has eroded. He knows it is not the mosquito that is to blame but his poverty. The mosquito is only the occasion. A man can be so helpless that even a mosquito may remind him of it.

At that moment the craving for a smoke comes on. He pulls a Gopal bidi from under the pillow, holds it between his lips, and strikes a match. Gopal means cowherd, a picture of simple village life, but to Saiful this bidi is no memory of a village. It is the only comfort of his present. When the bidi catches, "the room-bound darkness runs about, wanting to flee." It is a fine image. Darkness is inert and still, and yet the writer watches it run. Probably this is Saiful's own seeing: in the light of the smoke, memories, fears, longings and despair all go darting about. A single line is enough to give us a lonely, restless mind.

The morning scene is one of the story's strongest. He sits up, rubs his eyes, ties his lungi below the navel, drapes a gamchha over his shoulder, takes a miswak twig of olive wood in his mouth and a cake of Lifebuoy soap in his hand, and walks into the roofless bathing shed. In a bucket of water he sees his face: puffy eyes, mosquito marks across the forehead, thin little bumps like the scratches of chickenpox. He thinks, "Looking at this ugly face is wasted time." There is deep self-contempt in that. But who made the body ugly? Not Saiful. Poverty, malnutrition, exhaustion, sleeplessness and mosquitoes did. For him time is money and money is staying alive. Every moment lost means arriving late and facing the owner's glare, and that fear hounds him constantly.

The bathing shed stays with the reader. The burning stench of an open mix of filth, the constant drags on the bidi, the spitting again and again, the throat gone dry in an empty stomach choked with smoke. The reader feels the physical discomfort, and through it understands Saiful's condition. A man who never sees the sun, never eats enough, never sleeps properly gives off a smell that is itself a kind of illness, and in that smell Saiful catches the scent of his own decline. A dry throat and a numbed mind are conditions of the body, and of the spirit too.

And yet, amid all this hardship, the story allows one lovely moment. Back from his bath, shaking out the wrung gamchha, Saiful steps into the room and sees his wife asleep in the morning light. He puts on a shirt over his vest and trousers over his underwear and tucks the shirt in. Combing his hair leisurely before the mirror, comb in hand, he thinks, "Not bad at all! A proper dandy!" and the whole room seems to fill with his smile. For this moment Saiful is happy and sure of himself. Who ever called him a dandy, and why, the story does not say. But this is a man who lives on twenty-five taka, bathes in an open shed, and coughs in the stink of it, and he is calling himself a gentleman. Is it confidence, or self-deception dressed up as confidence? Probably both. Saiful loves himself, so he finds a good man inside himself, even if that man does not match his actual life. That is why the moment is funny and sad at once. Then his eye falls on the mosquito bites on his face, and the smile fades, as though reality had stepped in to say that the spell ends here.

Runu comes in, having splashed water on her face, drops tea dust into the kettle and strains it into two enamel cups. The scene is quiet. Runu says little, she works. Before the last sip of his tea, Saiful looks up in surprise and says, "Look at your face, the mosquitoes have bitten you like there's no tomorrow!" There is love in it, but it comes out sideways. Seeing the marks on her face hurts him, yet he cannot say so directly, and he says it in a way that keeps worry and helplessness together.

Then comes the matter of the municipality. Runu says, "There's a drain right at the porch. The municipality could spray a little medicine in the middle of all this, but it won't." It is an ordinary remark with a whole political reality inside it. The municipality could spray and does not, because this is a slum by an open drain, probably not worth counting even in the arithmetic of votes, and not a road anyone important sees. At the edge of town, somewhere between Puranbazar and Muniganj, nobody is looking. Mridha makes no speech. The state, the municipality, the administration are not part of Saiful's life at all. They are far away and unseen, and that very invisibility is the reality of the people who live here.

On the subject of a new net, Runu says, "Forget it, it won't happen in two or three months." Saiful says, "It's not for us—" and leaves the sentence hanging. With a sideways glance at her rounded belly, Runu says the rest for him: the net is not for the two of them but for the child who is coming. Saiful understands it all perfectly and drinks the last of his tea. Both know what is needed, and both know there is no money, and still neither says a word. In that silence there is deep agreement, and just as deep a despair.

Saying "I'm off," Saiful leaves the house and hits the road at a run. Is the hurry about work, or about escaping Runu's silent gesture? Probably both. He cannot bear the pain in her eyes, and he has no power to take it away. So he runs, without looking back for even a moment.

The story ends on this line: "Struck by an unseen blow inside the cage of his chest, Saiful's feet leap forward, fast!" The whole force of the story is gathered here. What is the unseen blow? Fear, anxiety, duty, or a fierce will to live? Probably all of it: Runu's pregnancy, the child to come, the missing net, the missing money, another night of bites, the municipality's indifference, the owner's glare, the twenty-five taka. All of it together makes one unseen blow, and under it Saiful's feet still move, fast. There is a bitter irony in that "fast." Where is he going? To a hotel that pays twenty-five taka. And what waits there? A day of labour, the manager's abuse, stale rice, and at night the return to the same holed net. Still he goes, because going is the only way he has. If he stops he will fall, and if he falls, Runu, the child, and a pregnant wife marked with bites will all come down with him.

The last scene sends us back to the beginning. The story began with a mosquito net, the one with a dozen or more holes, and it ends on a net: "Sooner or later, a net fit for three to sleep under is needed, for Runu and the child to come." Beginning and end meet at one point, but only after a long journey. At the start the net was a broken thing. At the end it has become a dream, a duty, a father's first task. Saiful is luckless and fallen, but he is also a father, and that gives him a new strength. It is small, almost nothing against twenty-five taka, but it is strength all the same, and by it he keeps walking even as the blow lands inside his chest.

Mridha's language here is colloquial, yet it carries the density of literature. "A room inside a room, and inside it you lie down and die" is as much speech as it is poetry. "An unseen blow in the cage of the chest" is as much description as it is symbol. Sentence length shifts, short here, long there, and the pace of the story comes out of that shifting. The word choices stand out too: "shameless mosquito," "a thunderous slap," "the room-bound darkness runs about, wanting to flee," "a belly like a bloated carp," "biting that scorches the skin." They are not just words but carriers of feeling, and each holds one layer of Saiful's life.

In building the setting, Mridha leaves place deliberately blurred. Khulna, Bagerhat, Mongla and Chattogram are named, but the slum where the story happens has no name. That is not neglect but a choice. Slums like this stand at the edge of every town in Bangladesh and on the border of every district. Time is just as vague. The date "1990" appears at the end, but nothing inside the story fixes it. As if to say this story belongs to no one moment but to all of them, and that is its greatest strength, because it is true today. The net Saiful needed in 1990 is a net countless Saifuls need still, and no one has counted them.

A word about the ending. Saiful is moving fast, but where he will arrive is not said. The story stops in the middle of motion, not at a conclusion, and that is its larger truth, because Saiful's life has not ended. Tomorrow he will get up again, go again to the bathing shed with its stench, drink tea from an enamel cup, run to the hotel for twenty-five taka, and come back again beneath the holed net. Runu's child will be born one day, and then? Will a new net be found for the baby? Will the owner open his hand and give the money? Will Saiful's feet go faster still, or one day stop? The story gives no answers, and in that absence of answers it finds its deepest human meaning.

What Mridha has done is tell of one very ordinary man's very ordinary night, and out of that ordinariness bring up a truth that stays with the reader long after the last page. "Moshari" is remembered for its simplicity. There is no complicated structure, no ornament, no unreal event. One man, one night, one mosquito net, one dream. Yet the depth within that simplicity hums in the mind for a long time. A holed net does not merely keep out mosquitoes. It becomes the sign of a whole life, and so exact a sign that, when the story is over, the reader feels he too once lay under that torn net on some night, was woken by the bites, and wondered: how much longer will this life go on?
